findings.body: The per-object name is passed into the metric's `kind` label position, producing unbounded metric cardinality and inconsistent labeling versus other methods which pass options.Kind.

findings.impact: The per-object name is passed into the metric's `kind` label position, producing unbounded metric cardinality and inconsistent labeling versus other methods which pass options.Kind.
findings.root_cause: Wrong argument supplied for the kind label of the storage duration metric.

findings.title: Delete storage duration uses object name as kind label
findings.verifier_reason: Line 106 shows `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` where `name` (object name) is passed as the kind label. Other methods pass `options.Kind`. This creates unbounded cardinality. The patch introduces this inconsistency.

pr.body:
**What is this feature?**

Mode 3 will work the following way:

reads (get, list) : only use unified storage
writes (create, update, delete, delete-collection) : write to unified storage and then asynchronously, write to legacy, just as a safe measure.

**Why do we need this feature?**

[Add a description of the problem the feature is trying to solve.]

**Who is this feature for?**

[Add information on what kind of user the feature is for.]

**Which issue(s) does this PR fix?**:

Fixes https://github.com/grafana/search-and-storage-team/issues/53

raw_findings.body: The context carries d.Log without the name/kind/method values just built into `log`, so downstream log lines lose the Delete-specific context, unlike Create/List/Update/DeleteCollection which install `log`.
raw_findings.failure_mode: Log entries missing intended structured fields.
raw_findings.impact: The context carries d.Log without the name/kind/method values just built into `log`, so downstream log lines lose the Delete-specific context, unlike Create/List/Update/DeleteCollection which install `log`.
raw_findings.root_cause: Base logger d.Log placed into context instead of the enriched `log`.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Use ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log) to propagate the enriched logger.
raw_findings.title: Delete builds enriched logger but installs base logger into context
raw_findings.trigger: Any Mode3 Delete call where downstream code reads the logger via klog.FromContext.

raw_findings.body: The derived context is cancelled as soon as the request completes, so the asynchronous legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection frequently aborts with context canceled, defeating the intended 'safe measure' legacy write.
raw_findings.evidence: ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))
raw_findings.failure_mode: Legacy writes silently cancelled, causing legacy store to diverge from unified store.
raw_findings.impact: The derived context is cancelled as soon as the request completes, so the asynchronous legacy Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection frequently aborts with context canceled, defeating the intended 'safe measure' legacy write.
raw_findings.root_cause: Async goroutine reuses the request-scoped context which is cancelled when the synchronous handler returns.
raw_findings.suggested_fix: Derive the goroutine context from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a fresh background context) before applying the timeout.
raw_findings.title: Async legacy writes use request context that is cancelled on return
raw_findings.trigger: The HTTP handler returns immediately after the storage write while the legacy write goroutine is still running; the apiserver cancels the request context.

finding.title: Async legacy writes use request context that is cancelled on return
finding.trigger: The HTTP handler returns immediately after the storage write while the legacy write goroutine is still running; the apiserver cancels the request context.
finding.verifier_reason: The claim that request context cancellation defeats async legacy writes is speculative. The goroutine creates its own timeout context with `context.WithTimeoutCause`. While parent cancellation propagates, this is standard Go context behavior and the 10-second timeout provides the intended window. No concrete evidence the apiserver cancels immediately upon return.
